idiom_name: record `with` expression plus a single reference store
implementation_notes: C# does not allow overloading the assignment operator, so the classic structure cannot exist; what remains is its ordering, and the language supplies it: a record (or a With... method on a class) builds a complete new instance through its generated copy constructor and with-expression, and the caller publishes it with one reference assignment, so nothing observes a half-built value and a failure inside the copy or the initializer leaves every existing reference untouched. Use init-only properties and immutable collections (ImmutableArray<T>) so the new instance is genuinely independent; for a class, a copy constructor plus init-only setters or WithX methods gives the same shape. Hand-written 'copy fields into a temp, then write them back' has no place here: assignment rebinds a reference, and mutating state a reader already holds defeats the guarantee.
pitfalls: Records are only shallowly immutable: a with-expression copies the reference of a List<T> member, so mutating that list through the copy is visible through the original -- store ImmutableArray<T> or copy in the constructor.

The generated copy constructor copies fields and the with-expression then runs the initializer, so computed properties or cached derived state can end up inconsistent; keep records to plain data and validate invariants in the constructor.

Copy-and-replace is not free: each update allocates a new record and copies every immutable collection it touches; in a hot loop, build a local draft and publish once instead of allocating per property.

variants.name: immutable state behind one reference field, committed with an atomic exchange
variants.idiom_name: Interlocked.Exchange / Volatile.Write publish of a freshly built state
variants.implementation_notes: When the state is read concurrently, keep it immutable and hold it in a single reference field; the writer builds the replacement and commits it with one atomic store -- Interlocked.Exchange(ref _state, next) when the previous value is needed, Volatile.Write when it is not, and CompareExchange in a retry loop when several writers compete. The exchange is the swap step: it cannot fail, the field always points at a complete state, and a reader that already loaded the old reference keeps a consistent snapshot while the collector reclaims it. Prefer this variant to the with-expression form when readers must run lock-free; the costs are an allocation per update and the rule that published state is never mutated afterwards.
pitfalls: Interlocked.Exchange is atomic for the field, not for a read-modify-write sequence: Load followed by Exchange loses concurrent updates unless CompareExchange retries.
Interlocked and Volatile take a reference or a primitive; passing a struct copies it, so the commit silently degrades to a non-atomic struct write.
Letting this escape the constructor (or writing a non-readonly field after construction) publishes a half-built object even when the store itself is atomic.
